ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In the microscopic world of a pond, paramecia are ferocious predators that prey on smaller protists. In a classic experiment, two species of paramecia were grown separately in culture. The species in culture A was P. caudatum. The species in culture B was P. bursaria. Then the two species were combined in one culture dish (culture C).

Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the growth pattern of the two populations combined in culture C?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: P.caudatum and P. bursaria occupy different niches.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: There are three growth-curve graphs in the figure. Graph A shows that when P. caudatum is cultured alone, the population density rises with the number of days and stabilizes near a higher level. Graph B shows that when P. bursaria is cultured alone, the population density also rises and stabilizes near a lower level. Graph C shows that when the two organisms are cultured together, there are two growth curves; both continue to exist and each reaches a stable population density, with no situation in which one of them drops to zero. Reasoning: If two species occupy exactly the same niche and compete for the same limiting resource, competitive exclusion usually occurs, causing one of the species to be excluded. But in Graph C the two can stably coexist, indicating that they are not using the same resource in exactly the same way. The most likely explanation is that P. caudatum and P. bursaria occupy different niches.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: identify the separate-culture growth curves in A and B and the combined-culture graph C. Note that in culture C both P. caudatum and P. bursaria persist and reach stable population densities instead of one declining to zero. Then connect this growth pattern to ecology: stable coexistence means they are not competing for exactly the same limiting resources in the same way. Therefore the most likely explanation is that P. caudatum and P. bursaria occupy different ecological niches.
